what_this_is: The per-check AXIS DECOMPOSITION for the OC checks C1a's crosswalk lands an edge on and A3 did NOT decompose. A3 committed 13 of the 175; its scope block hands the other 162 to C1. This file holds C1a's share of them and nothing else.
why_a_second_file_and_not_an_edit_of_A3s: Editing docs/conformance/oc-axes-2026-07-28.json would give one artefact two owners — the MES-24 two-censuses defect, where the two disagree and nothing detects it. A3 owns its 13; C1 owns what C1 extracts. Disjointness is ASSERTED BY THE BUILDER (mix conformance.crosswalk refuses on any overlap), not left to a convention. PM-ratified as D4, MES-97 comment 27858.
axis_source_rule: AXES COME FROM THE PREDICATE, NEVER FROM THE DESCRIPTION — docs/conformance/match-relation.md §2, cited not restated.
difference_from_A3s_13: A3's 13 are all `a(...)`-form checks whose predicate is an inline arrow function, so every axis expression is a substring of the emitting excerpt itself. NONE of the checks here is like that: every one computes its predicate into a minified binding BEFORE the emitting call, and three of them are decided at a site that is not the emitting site at all. So each row carries `context_excerpts` — further addressed spans the predicate depends on — and an axis `expr` is a verbatim substring of the evaluator excerpt OR of one of them. The row says which, in `expr_found_in`.

provenance.emitting_spans_from: docs/conformance/oc-emitting-sites-2026-07-28.json — generated by mix conformance.locator, not re-cut by hand
provenance.context_spans_from: located by unique-substring search against the same build; each is unique in it
provenance.bytes_are_not_stored_here: Spans only. `mix conformance.crosswalk` lifts the bytes LIVE from the build at these spans and refuses if any axis `expr` is not a verbatim substring of what it lifted. Storing the bytes here as well would create a second copy that can drift from the build without anything noticing — the same reasoning bucket-0 gives for lifting rather than remembering.

polarity_rule: `pass_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the passing arm. `fail_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the failing arm. Read off the branch the excerpt actually writes, never off the requirement's wording.
preconditions_rule: A list of `{guard, kind, on_failure, reads}`. A precondition is NOT an axis: its failure does not make the check fail, it makes the check not evaluate (SKIPPED). An ET claim cannot agree or contradict a precondition, so `shape_from_axes/1` never sees one.

scope.population: The OC checks C1a's and C1b-i's declared populations land an edge on, minus the one A3 already decomposed. C1a contributed 11 (request-metadata, MRTR and tools_call); C1b-i contributes the 29 CG7 checks — `http-custom-headers` 18 + `http-invalid-tool-headers` 11 — ALL of them, including the 9 that carry no ET-CC edge, because a bucket-2 check must be decomposed before it can be shown to have no counterpart.
scope.the_one_A3_already_has: sep-2575-http-server-method-not-found-404-initialize / HttpServerMethodNotFound404initialize — C1a's 12th check. Read from A3's file, NOT re-extracted here. One fact, one home.
scope.not_decomposed: The remaining 132 of the 173. They are C1b-ii's, C1b-iii's (MES-104's siblings) and C1c's (MES-105).

key: Client declares valid roots capability if present

context_excerpts.label: capability_helper
context_excerpts.why: the emitting site is a call to the helper `f`; the predicate is in the helper body, not at the call

context_excerpts.label: capabilities_binding
context_excerpts.why: binds `d`, the declared capability map the helper reads

axes.polarity_reading: `r=typeof t==`object`&&t&&!Array.isArray(t)?`SUCCESS`:`FAILURE``
axes.requires: the declared `roots` capability value is a non-null, non-array object

conjunct_grouping.why: THREE conjuncts, ONE axis, and this is a reading rather than a mechanical split — so it is recorded rather than buried. In JavaScript `typeof null === 'object'` and `typeof [] === 'object'`, so the second and third conjuncts are REPAIRS of the first's idiom, not separate required behaviours. Splitting them would create two axes an ET claim could be 'silent' on that name no behaviour a test could assert separately, and `partial` would then be reported over an artefact of the language. D may regroup: the conjuncts are listed verbatim so it does not have to re-cut the site.

preconditions.reads: whether the client declared a `roots` capability at all; the check scores its SHAPE, never its presence

key: Client retries with a supported version when first choice is rejected

context_excerpts.label: status_mutation_site
context_excerpts.why: THE PREDICATE IS HERE, NOT AT THE EMITTING SITE — see emitting_site_is_not_the_predicate below

checks.emitting_site_is_not_the_predicate: The emitting excerpt writes `status:`WARNING`` as a CONSTANT: it seeds the check before the retry has happened. The verdict is decided 221 bytes later, where `this.checks.find(...)` re-reads the row and overwrites its status. A consumer who follows the locator to the emitting site and stops reads a literal and finds no predicate at all — recorded as S9-16, and it is why this row carries a context excerpt rather than a wider emitting span.

axes.polarity_reading: `o===`2026-07-28`&&a===`2026-07-28`?p.status=`SUCCESS`:p.status=`WARNING``
axes.requires: the retry's MCP-Protocol-Version header names the version the server offered

axes.polarity_reading: the second conjunct of the same ternary test
axes.requires: the retry's `_meta` protocolVersion names the version the server offered

checks.conjunction_note: TWO axes: the ternary tests header AND _meta independently, and a client could re-stamp one without the other. That is not hypothetical — MES-97's declared population contains a member asserting exactly that lockstep.

key: Client MUST echo back the exact value of requestState when retrying

context_excerpts.label: error_accumulator
context_excerpts.why: the predicate is `l.length===0` and `l` is an error list; the conditions that push into it ARE the axes

axes.expr: l.push(`Client did not include requestState in retry`)
axes.polarity_reading: the ELSE arm of `i?...:...` — reached when the retry carried no requestState, and it pushes an error
axes.requires: when the server sent a requestState, the retry includes one

axes.polarity_reading: `i?i!==c&&l.push(...)` — inequality with what the server sent pushes an error
axes.requires: the echoed requestState is byte-identical to the one the server sent — not inspected, parsed or modified

checks.error_accumulator_note: The status expression is `l.length===0`, so the axes are the error PUSHES, not the status expression. Reading `l.length===0` as one axis would collapse two independently-failing behaviours into one and lose the distinction the harness's own two error messages draw.

key: If InputRequiredResult does not contain requestState, client MUST NOT include one in the retry

context_excerpts.label: error_accumulator
context_excerpts.why: binds `a` and holds the single guarded push that decides the status

axes.polarity_reading: `n!==void 0&&a.push(...)` — a requestState present when none was sent pushes an error
axes.requires: when the server sent no requestState, the retry carries none — not an empty one, not a null one

key: Validates that the add_numbers tool works correctly

axes.polarity_reading: first conjunct of `n=e!==void 0&&...`, and `status:n?`SUCCESS`:`FAILURE``
axes.requires: the client issued a `tools/call` at all

axes.polarity_reading: second conjunct of the same `&&` chain
axes.requires: the call's `a` argument is sent as a JSON number, not a string

axes.polarity_reading: third conjunct of the same `&&` chain
axes.requires: the call's `b` argument is sent as a JSON number, not a string

checks.conjunction_note: THREE axes, and unlike the capability rows these are NOT one behaviour spelled three ways: a client can call the tool and mistype one argument, and the three conjuncts fail independently. Grouping them would hide a real partial.
checks.not_scored_by_the_check: The excerpt computes `result:t.a+t.b` in its DETAILS, but no conjunct tests it. The check scores that the call was made with two numeric arguments — never that the answer was right. A reader going by the description ('Validates that the add_numbers tool works correctly') would score us against arithmetic the predicate does not test. A3 §2's rule, on the check this population happens to include.

emitting_span_provenance_rule: Every row states where its `emitting_byte_span` came from, and the generator CHECKS the statement against MES-97's locator output (G18). `locator_row` — the span is one the locator names for this row's key, and the generator requires that. `locator_row_rejected` — the locator's own `rung_pin_level` for that row is NOT `row`, so it does not claim to pin the row; the span it names belongs to a sibling and is refused. The generator then requires the reverse: the pin level must not be `row`, the span used must NOT be one of the locator's, and a reason must be given. Four of C1b-i's 29 rows are rejections; C1a's 11 are all `locator_row`, and were so before this field existed.
check_id_location_rule: C1a's 11 rows all carry their check id as a backtick literal at the emitting site, and the generator required exactly that. Fourteen of C1b-i's rows emit with `id:c` — a value COMPUTED from the argument's value and declared type — and ten more with `id:t`, a loop variable. So a row may name `check_id_found_in`: the pool entry whose bytes must carry the id literal. It defaults to `evaluator_excerpt`, which is C1a's behaviour unchanged, and the named entry must exist. This WEAKENS the guard from `the id is at the emitting site` to `the id is verbatim at an ADDRESSED span this row names`, and that is said plainly rather than left to be noticed: what it still refuses is a row whose id occurs nowhere it points at.
